questions.q: What does Dynamic Data Masking (DDM) actually change?
options: The values returned in a query's result set, in real time, based on who's asking — the actual stored data is never modified
The physical bytes stored on disk for the masked column
The encryption algorithm used for the entire database
The firewall rules governing who can connect to the server
questions.explain: DDM assumes the query is legitimate and the data is already flowing normally — it rewrites only what a class of user is allowed to see.

questions.q: What permission controls whether a user sees real, unmasked values on a masked column?
options: UNMASK
db_owner, automatically and unconditionally
CONTROL SERVER
ALTER ANY MASK
questions.explain: GRANT UNMASK TO a principal lets them see real values; everyone else sees masked output regardless of other permissions they hold.

questions.q: Which masking function type replaces a numeric value with a plausible but fake number within a defined range?
options: Random
Default
Email
Partial
questions.explain: Random masking is commonly used for numeric columns like salary, substituting a fake but plausible value in a configured range.

questions.q: Why is Dynamic Data Masking described as a "least-exposure" control rather than a real security boundary?
options: A user with enough query permission can often infer or extract real values through workarounds, such as filtering on the real value in a WHERE clause, since masking only rewrites the displayed result, not the underlying data being evaluated
Because DDM actually encrypts the underlying data using the same mechanism as Always Encrypted
Because DDM requires Transparent Data Encryption to be disabled first
Because masked columns cannot be queried at all by any user
questions.explain: Microsoft's own guidance is that DDM should be combined with proper permissions and auditing, not relied on as the sole control for truly sensitive data.

questions.q: How does DDM's threat model differ from TDE and Always Encrypted's threat model?
options: DDM assumes the querying user already has legitimate access and the data is already decrypted and flowing normally; TDE and Always Encrypted assume the accessor should have no access at all
They all address the exact same threat model with different implementations
DDM protects against storage theft, the same as TDE
Always Encrypted and DDM both require the same Column Master Key
questions.explain: This is the key conceptual distinction across Lessons 31-33: different tools for different classes of threat.
